lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Pollux, I have a commission for you. As soon as you get upstairs — it is your turn back among the living tomorrow, I think — if you happen to see Menippus the Dog, and you’ll find him in Corinth by the Craneion, or in the Lyceum laughing at the philosophers arguing with each other, tell him this: “Menippus, Diogenes says that if you have had enough laughing at things above ground, come down here. There is much more to laugh at.”

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Up there the joke still had a certain uncertainty about it — all that “Who really knows what comes after life?” business. Down here you can laugh with confidence, as I do now. Especially when you see the rich men, satraps, and tyrants brought so low and so anonymous that you can only identify them by the wailing, and by how soft and sorry they are whenever they remember upstairs.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell him that. And add that he should come with his bag full: plenty of lupins, and if he finds a supper laid out for Hecate at a crossroads, or an egg from a purification, or anything of that kind, bring that too.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: I’ll deliver it, Diogenes. But so I can recognize him properly — what does he look like?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Old. Bald. Wearing a little cloak with more doors than a tenement, open to every wind, patterned by the overlapping patches of rags. He is always laughing, and most of the time he is needling those fraud philosophers.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: On that description, he should be easy to find.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Would you like me to give you a message for those philosophers themselves?

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: Go on. That is no great burden either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: In general, tell them from me to stop talking nonsense: stop quarrelling about the universe, stop growing horns on each other, stop making crocodiles, and stop teaching the mind to ask insoluble little riddles of that sort.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: They’ll say I’m ignorant and uneducated if I attack their wisdom.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then tell them from me to go howl.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: I’ll deliver that too, Diogenes.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the rich, my dear Pollux, take this message from us: “Why are you guarding the gold, you idiots? Why punish yourselves calculating the interest, piling talent on talent, when in a little while you must arrive here with one obol?”

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: That shall be said to them as well.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And tell the beautiful and the strong — Megillus of Corinth, for instance, and Damoxenus the wrestler — that with us there is no blond hair, no grey eyes or black eyes, no blush in the face, no springy sinews, no mighty shoulders. It is all one dust here, as they say: skulls stripped bare of beauty.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: That won’t be hard to say to the beautiful and the strong.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And to the poor, Spartan — there are plenty of them, taking the matter hard and pitying themselves for their poverty — tell them not to cry and not to wail. Explain the equality down here, and that they will see the rich from up there no better off than themselves.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And if you like, scold your Spartans for me as well. Tell them they have gone slack.

lines.speaker: Pollux
lines.text: No, Diogenes. Say nothing about the Spartans. I will not stand for that. But the messages to the others — those I’ll deliver.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: We’ll leave them alone, since you prefer it. Just carry the speeches I gave you to the people I named.
